user_input: A trial court convicts a person of an offence that allows punishment with both imprisonment and fine. The court imposes a fine but does not specify any maximum amount in the judgment. The person does not pay the fine. What limits apply to (i) how large the fine can be, and (ii) what kind of imprisonment the court may order in default of payment?

( 2 ) In every case of an offence -
( a ) punishable with imprisonment as well as fine, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine, whether with or without imprisonment;
( b ) punishable with imprisonment or fine, or with fine only, in which the offender is sentenced to a fine,

it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct by the sentence that, in default of payment of the fine, the offender shall suffer imprisonment for a certain term, in which imprisonment shall be in excess of any other imprisonment to which he may have been sentenced or to which he may be liable under a commutation of a sentence.
( 3 ) The term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned in default of payment of a fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which is the maximum fixed for the offence, if the offence be punishable with imprisonment as well as fine.
( 4 )  The  imprisonment  which  the  Court  imposes  in  default  of  payment  of  a  fine  or  in  default  of community service may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.
( 5 )  If the offence is punishable with fine or community service, the imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of the fine or in default of community service shall be simple, and the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned, in default of payment of fine or in default of community service, shall not exceed, -
( a ) two months when the amount of the fine does not exceed five thousand rupees;
( b ) four months when the amount of the fine does not exceed ten thousand rupees; and
- ( c ) one year in any other case.
( 6 ) ( a ) The imprisonment which is imposed in default of payment of a fine shall terminate whenever that fine is either paid or levied by process of law;
( b )  If,  before  the  expiration  of  the  term  of  imprisonment  fixed  in  default  of  payment,  such  a proportion of the fine be paid or levied that the term of imprisonment suffered in default of payment is not less than proportional to the part of the fine still unpaid, the imprisonment shall terminate.', 'Imprisonment  for  non-payment  of  fine,  when  offence  punishable  with  fine  only . -If  the offence be punishable with fine only, 1 [the imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of the fine shall be simple, and] the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned, in default of payment of fine, shall not exceed the following scale, that is to say, for any term not exceeding two months when the amount of the fine shall not exceed fifty rupees, and for any term not exceeding four months when the amount shall not exceed one hundred rupees, and for any term not exceeding six months in any other case.', 'Description of imprisonment for non-payment of fine . -The imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of a fine may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence.', 'Imprisonment  to  terminate  on  payment  of  fine . -The  imprisonment  which  is  imposed  in default of payment of a fine shall terminate whenever that fine is either paid or levied by process of law.']
response:
(i) **How large the fine can be (no maximum stated):**  
If **no sum is expressed to which a fine may extend**, then “**the amount of fine to which the offender is liable is unlimited, but shall not be excessive**.” [2]

(ii) **Imprisonment in default of payment (offence punishable with imprisonment as well as fine):**  
For an offence “**punishable with imprisonment as well as fine**” where the offender “**is sentenced to a fine**,” the court may direct that “**in default of payment of the fine, the offender shall suffer imprisonment for a certain term**” and this imprisonment must be “**in excess of any other imprisonment to which he may have been sentenced**” (and any imprisonment liable under commutation). [2]  
Additionally, “**the term for which the Court directs the offender to be imprisoned in default of payment of a fine shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which is the maximum fixed for the offence**.” [2]  

**Kind/description of imprisonment:**  
“The imprisonment which the Court imposes in default of payment of a fine … **may be of any description to which the offender might have been sentenced for the offence**.” [2]
reference: The fine is not limited by any stated maximum, but it must not be excessive. In default of payment, the court may direct imprisonment for a certain term, and that default imprisonment must be in excess of any other imprisonment the offender has been sentenced to or may be liable to under commutation.

The grievous hurt is committed in consequence of B’s instigation, but the Code does not separately provide a specific punishment for B’s abetment of this particular outcome. A is guilty of abetting that offence by conspiracy, and is liable to the punishment for murder."]
response:
B would be punished for the offence committed by A “in consequence” of B’s instigation, even though the Code does not separately provide a specific punishment for this particular outcome. Under the rule on “Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment,” the abettor is “liable to the same punishment” as the person who commits the offence, as shown in the illustrations (e.g., where A instigates B and B commits the offence in consequence, A is “liable to the same punishment as B”). [4]

Here, A voluntarily causes grievous hurt only if he “both causes grievous hurt and intends or knows himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt,” and the definition allows that “if intending or knowing himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt of one kind, he actually causes grievous hurt of another kind.” [3]

So, applying the abetment rule: since A’s grievous hurt was “in consequence” of B’s instigation and there is no separate express punishment for B’s abetment of that outcome, B should face liability with reference to the same punishment applicable to A’s offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt (not a different punishment based on the mismatch between B’s intention for theft and A’s intention/knowledge regarding grievous hurt). [4,3]
reference: B should be punished for the offence that would have been committed if A had acted with B’s intention/knowledge (i.e., the theft intended by B), and also, since the act abetted (grievous hurt) was committed in consequence of the abetment and there is no express provision for punishment of that abetment, B is punished with the punishment provided for the offence actually committed.

user_input: What is the exact phrase used to describe the act of making or publishing an imputation intended to harm or likely to harm a person’s reputation?

['Defamation . -Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.', 'Defamation. -( 1 ) Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible  representations,  makes  or  publishes  in  any  manner,  any  imputation  concerning  any  person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.', "Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loothsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.", "Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loathsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.", "Ins. by Act 46 of 1983, s. 2 (w.e.f. 25-12-1983).
Explanation 1. -It  may  amount  to  defamation  to  impute  anything  to  a  deceased  person,  if  the imputation would harm the reputation of that person if living, and is intended to be hurtful to the fellings of his family or other near relatives.
Explanation 2. -It  may amount to defamation to make an imputation concerning a company or an association or collection of persons as such.
Explanation 3. -An imputation in the form of an alternative or expressed ironically, may amount to defamation.
Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loothsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.
Illustrations
( a ) A says -' Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch ' ; intending to cause it to be believed that Z did steal B's watch. This is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
( b )  A  is  asked  who  stole  B's  watch.  A  points  to  Z,  intending  to  cause  it  to  be  believed  that  Z  stole  B's  watch.  This  is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
( c )  A  draws  a  picture  of  Z  running  away  with  B's  watch,  intending  it  to  be  believed  that  Z  stole  B's  watch.  This  is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
First Exception . -Imputation of truth which public good requires to be made or published . -It is not defamation to impute anything which is true concerning any person, if it be for the public good that the imputation should be made or published. Whether or not it is for the public good is a question of fact.
Second Exception . -Public  conduct  of  public  servants . -It  is  not  defamation  to  express  in  good faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the  conduct  of  a  public  servant  in  the  discharge  of  his  public functions, or respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Third Exception . -Conduct of any person touching any public question . -It is not defamation to express in  good  faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the  conduct  of  any  person  touching  any  public question, and respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Illustration
It is not defamation in A to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting Z's conduct in petitioning Government on a  public  question,  in  signing  a  requisition  for  a  meeting  on  a  public  question,  in  presiding  or  attending  at  such  meeting,  in forming  or  joining  any  society  which  invites  the  public  support,  in  voting  or  canvassing  for  a  particular  candidate  for  any situation in the efficient discharge of the duties of which the public is interested.
Explanation . -A Justice of the Peace or other officer holding an enquiry in open Court preliminary to a trial in a Court of Justice, is a Court within the meaning of the above section.
Fourth  Exception . -Publication  of  reports  of  proceedings  of  courts. -It  is  not  defamation  to publish  substantially  true  report  of  the  proceedings  of  a  Court  of  Justice,  or  of  the  result  of  any  such proceedings.
Fifth  Exception . -Merits  of case decided  in  Court  or  conduct  of witnesses and  others concerned . -It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the merits of any case, civil or criminal, which has been decided by a Court of Justice, or respecting the conduct of any person as a party, witness or agent, in any such case, or respecting the character of such person, as far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Illustrations
( b ) But if A says -' I do not believe what Z asserted at that trial because I know him to be a man without veracity ' ; A is not within this exception, inasmuch as the opinion which express of Z's character, is an opinion not founded on Z's conduct as a witness.
( a )  A  says -' I  think  Z's  evidence  on  that  trial  is  so  contradictory  that  he  must  be  stupid  or  dishonest. ' A  is  within  this exception if he says this in good faith, inasmuch as the opinion which he expresses respects Z's character as it appears in Z's conduct as a witness, and no farther.
Sixth Exception . -Merits of public performance . -It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion respecting the merits of any performance which its author has submitted to the judgment of the public, or respecting the character of the author so far as his character appears in such performance, and no further.
Explanation . -A performance may be submitted to the judgment of the public expressly or by acts on the part of the author which imply such submission to the judgment of the public.
- ( a ) A person who publishes a book, submits that book to the judgment of the public.
- ( b ) A person who makes a speech in public, submits that speech to the judgment of the public.
- ( c ) An actor or singer who appears on a public stage, submits his acting or singing to the judgment of the public.
( d ) A says of a book published by Z -' Z ' s book is foolish; Z must be a weak man. Z's book is indecent; Z must be a man of  impure  mind ' .  A  is  within  the  exception,  if  he  says  this  in  good  faith,  inasmuch  as  the  opinion  which  he  expresses  of  Z respects Z's character only so far as it appears in Z's book, and no further.
( e ) But if A says ' I am not surprised that Z's book is foolish and indecent, for he is a weak man and a libertine ' . A is not within this exception, in as much as the opinion which he expresses of Z's character is an opinion not founded on Z's book.
Illustrations
Seventh  Exception . -Censure  passed  in  good  faith  by  person  having  lawful  authority  over another . -It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.
Illustration
A Judge censuring in good faith the conduct of a witness, or of an officer of the Court; a head of a department censuring in good  faith  those  who  are  under  his  orders,  a  parent  censuring  in  good  faith  a  child  in  the  presence  of  other  children;  a schoolmaster, whose authority is derived from a parent, censuring in good faith a pupil in the presence of other pupils; a master censuring  a  servant  in  good  faith  for  remissness  in  service;  a  banker  censuring  in  good  faith  the  cashier  of  his  bank  for  the conduct of such cashier as such cashier- are within this exception.
Eighth Exception . -Accusation preferred in good  faith to authorised  person . -It is not defamation  to  prefer  in  good  faith  an  accusation  against  any  person  to  any  of  those  who  have  lawful authority over that person with respect to the subject-matter of accusation.
If A in good faith accuses Z before a Magistrate; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a servant, to Z's master; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a child, to Z's father-A is within this exception.
Ninth  Exception . -Imputation  made  in  good  faith  by  person  for  protection  of  his  or  other's interests . -It  is  not  defamation  to  make  an  imputation  on  the  character  of  another  provided  that  the imputation be made in good faith for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good.
Illustrations
( a ) A, a shopkeeper, says to B, who manages his business -' Sell nothing to Z unless he pays you ready money, for I have no opinion of his honesty. ' A is within the exception, if he has made this imputation on Z in good faith for the protection of his own interests.
( b ) A, a Magistrate, in making a report to his own superior officer, casts an imputation on the character of Z. Here, if the imputation is made in good faith, and for the public good, A is within the exception.
Tenth Exception . -Caution intended for good of person to whom conveyed or for public good . -It is not defamation to convey a caution, in good faith, to one person against another, provided that such caution be intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed, or of some person in whom that person is interested, or for the public good."]
response: The exact phrase is: “**makes or publishes any imputation** … **intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person**” [1]

**For A (false criminal complaint with intent to cause injury; false charge; alleges an offence punishable with death):**  
Under **BNS §248(a)–(b)**, where A “**with intent to cause injury… institutes or causes to be instituted any criminal proceeding… or falsely charges**” a person, knowing there is no just or lawful ground, and where the false proceeding/charge is “**punishable with death**,” the maximum is:  
- **Imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years**; and  
- **fine is also applicable** (“**and shall also be liable to fine**”) [4].

**For C (assists B to avoid legal punishment by hiding him; screening from punishment):**  
On the given facts (C “**helps B by hiding**” so B can “**avoid legal punishment**”), **BNS §238** applies for causing disappearance of evidence or giving false information **with the intention of screening the offender from legal punishment**. The maximum term depends on the alleged offence punishable with death. For an offence punishable with death, **BNS §238(a)** provides:  
- **Imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years**; and  
- **fine is also applicable** (“**shall also be liable to fine**”) [1].

**Answer (maximums):**  
- **A:** up to **10 years’ imprisonment**; **fine also applicable** [4].  
- **C:** up to **7 years’ imprisonment**; **fine also applicable** [1].
reference: A can be punished with imprisonment up to 7 years and also be liable to fine. C, for harbouring/concealing an offender to screen him from legal punishment where the underlying offence is punishable with death, can be punished with imprisonment up to 5 years and also be liable to fine.

A  is  within  the  exception,  if  he  has  made  this imputation on Z in good faith for the protection of his own interests.\n( b )  A,  a  Magistrate,  in  making  a  report  to  his  own  superior  officer,  casts  an  imputation  on  the character of Z. Here, if the imputation is made in good faith, and for the public good, A is within the exception."]

Based on the facts given, the conduct most directly attracts **BNS §341 (Making or possessing counterfeit seal, etc.)** for counterfeit seals, and **IPC §487 (Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods)** for false marks on product packaging.

## 1) BNS §341 — counterfeit seal (making/possessing/using)
- **If he made or counterfeited the seal** intending it to be used for dishonest/forgery-type purposes, BNS §341(2) applies: punishment is **imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years**, and **shall also be liable to fine**. [4]
- **If he used the counterfeit seal as genuine knowing (or having reason to believe) it to be counterfeit**, BNS §341(4) applies: punishment is **“in the same manner as if he had made or counterfeited”** such seal. [1]
  - Since BNS §341(2) provides the higher maximum (**up to seven years + fine**), using the counterfeit seal as genuine would carry the same maximum exposure. [1, 4]
- **If he possessed a counterfeit seal knowing it to be counterfeit**, BNS §341(3) applies: **imprisonment of either description up to three years**, **and shall also be liable to fine**. [3]

### Effect of his “no intent to defraud” defense
BNS §341(2) expressly turns on **“intending that the same shall be used for the purpose of committing any forgery”** (and possession “with such intent” plus knowledge the seal is counterfeit). The provided context does not state an exemption where the defendant claims he did not intend to defraud. [4]

So, on the given facts (printing/applying an identical “Genuine” seal and selling as genuine), the **maximum** exposure under BNS §341 is:
- **Up to seven years’ imprisonment + fine** (via BNS §341(2), and reinforced by BNS §341(4)’s “same manner” rule). [4, 1]

## 2) IPC §487 — false mark on product receptacles
IPC §487 punishes making a **false mark** on any case/package/receptacle containing goods, in a manner reasonably calculated to cause others to believe the receptacle contains goods it does not contain, or that the goods are of a different nature/quality than they truly are.

Punishment (unless he proves he acted without intent to defraud):
- **imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years**, **or with fine, or with both**. [2]

### His defense about no intent to defraud
IPC §487 includes: **“unless he proves that he acted without intent to defraud”**. The context does not say whether he can or does prove this, only that it is a requirement to avoid liability under §487. [2]

So, the **maximum** exposure under IPC §487 is:
- **Up to three years’ imprisonment, or fine, or both**. [2]

## Maximum punishment (from the provided context)
- **Maximum under BNS §341:** **up to seven years’ imprisonment + fine**. [4, 1]
- **Maximum under IPC §487:** **up to three years’ imprisonment, or fine, or both (absent proof of no intent to defraud).** [2]
reference: He can be held liable for using a false property mark and for counterfeiting a property mark used by another. The maximum punishment for using a false property mark is up to 1 year imprisonment (or fine, or both), unless he proves he acted without intent to defraud; the maximum punishment for counterfeiting another person’s property mark is up to 2 years imprisonment (or fine, or both).

Here, though A and B are both engaged in causing Z's death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.", 'Robbery. -( 1 ) In all robbery there is either theft or extortion.

This is extortion, and punishable as such: but it is not robbery, unless Z is put in fear of the instant death of his child.", "Subs. by Act 26 of 1955, s. 117 and the Sch., for 'transportation for life' (w.e.f. 1 -1-1956).
When  theft  is  robbery . -Theft  is ' robbery ' if,  in  order  to  the  committing  of  the  theft,  or  in committing the theft, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by the theft, the offender,  for  that  end  voluntarily  causes  or  attempts  to  cause  to  any  person  death  or  hurt  or  wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death or of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint.

Yes.

1) **Guard and transporter liability (even without breaking the cash box):**  
Under **BNS §309(6)**, where any person **“in committing or in attempting to commit robbery, voluntarily causes hurt,”** liability for the robbery offence (and higher punishment) extends to **“such person, and any other person jointly concerned in committing or attempting to commit such robbery.”** [1]  
Also, the definition of robbery includes situations where theft is robbery if the offender, in relation to theft, voluntarily causes **death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death/instant hurt/instant wrongful restraint** and extortion is robbery when done **in the presence** of the person put in fear and causes them **“then and there to deliver up the thing extorted.”** [3]  
Given your facts describe the guard preventing intervention and the transporter helping move the stolen money as intentional acts **during the robbery**, they can be treated as **“jointly concerned”** persons in the robbery act. [1]

2) **Different members can be convicted for different offences arising from the same overall act:**  
Yes. **IPC §38** provides: **“Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be guilty of different offences by means of that act.”** [2]  

So, **the guard and transporter may be held liable for the robbery offence** as persons **jointly concerned**, and **different members may be convicted for different offences** arising from the same overall criminal act. [1, 2]
reference: Yes. If an offence is committed through several acts, anyone who intentionally cooperates by doing any one of those acts (alone or jointly) is liable for the offence. Also, where several persons are concerned in the same criminal act, different persons may be guilty of different offences by means of that act.

Yes. Under the provided provisions, the person who broke open the box can be criminally liable even though the theft was not completed, because criminal liability for a “criminal conspiracy” requires only that **“some act besides the agreement is done … in pursuance thereof”** [4]. Breaking open the box is an act **besides the original agreement** and (on your facts) done in pursuance of it, so it meets that threshold for conspiracy liability.  

As for the other person: **if they did nothing beyond the original agreement**, then the **agreement alone** is not enough to constitute criminal conspiracy in these documents, because **“no agreement … shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof.”** [4]
reference: Yes. The person who broke open the box has done an act towards committing theft and can be held liable for attempt even though nothing was found. The other person, having only agreed and done no act beyond the agreement in pursuance of it, is not liable for criminal conspiracy.

Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loothsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.

Eighth Exception . -Accusation preferred in good  faith to authorised  person . -It is not defamation  to  prefer  in  good  faith  an  accusation  against  any  person  to  any  of  those  who  have  lawful authority over that person with respect to the subject-matter of accusation.
If A in good faith accuses Z before a Magistrate; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a servant, to Z's master; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a child, to Z's father-A is within this exception.
Ninth  Exception . -Imputation  made  in  good  faith  by  person  for  protection  of  his  or  other's interests . -It  is  not  defamation  to  make  an  imputation  on  the  character  of  another  provided  that  the imputation be made in good faith for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good.
Illustrations
( a ) A, a shopkeeper, says to B, who manages his business -' Sell nothing to Z unless he pays you ready money, for I have no opinion of his honesty. ' A is within the exception, if he has made this imputation on Z in good faith for the protection of his own interests.
( b ) A, a Magistrate, in making a report to his own superior officer, casts an imputation on the character of Z. Here, if the imputation is made in good faith, and for the public good, A is within the exception.
Tenth Exception . -Caution intended for good of person to whom conveyed or for public good . -It is not defamation to convey a caution, in good faith, to one person against another, provided that such caution be intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed, or of some person in whom that person is interested, or for the public good."]
response:
A person can avoid liability for defamation when the imputation about another’s character is made **“in good faith”** for one of the permitted purposes—namely **“for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good.”** [3]

So, to avoid liability, it must be shown that:
- **Purpose:** the imputation was made in **good faith** to protect **the person’s own interests**, **someone else’s interests**, or **the public good** [3]; and
- **Manner (as stated in the exception):** the imputation must be **made** under that good-faith protective/public-good purpose (the context does not add further manner requirements beyond this). [3]
reference: Defamation is not committed if the imputation about another’s character is made in good faith for protecting the interests of the person making it, or of another person, or for the public good.

Explanation 4. -No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or  indirectly,  in  the  estimation  of  others,  lowers  the  moral  or  intellectual  character  of  that  person,  or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person,  or  causes  it  to  be  believed  that  the  body  of  that  person  is  in  a  loothsome  state,  or  in  a  state generally considered as disgraceful.
Illustrations
( a ) A says -' Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch ' ; intending to cause it to be believed that Z did steal B's watch. This is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
( b )  A  is  asked  who  stole  B's  watch.  A  points  to  Z,  intending  to  cause  it  to  be  believed  that  Z  stole  B's  watch.  This  is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
( c )  A  draws  a  picture  of  Z  running  away  with  B's  watch,  intending  it  to  be  believed  that  Z  stole  B's  watch.  This  is defamation, unless it fall within one of the exceptions.
First Exception . -Imputation of truth which public good requires to be made or published . -It is not defamation to impute anything which is true concerning any person, if it be for the public good that the imputation should be made or published. Whether or not it is for the public good is a question of fact.
Second Exception . -Public  conduct  of  public  servants . -It  is  not  defamation  to  express  in  good faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the  conduct  of  a  public  servant  in  the  discharge  of  his  public functions, or respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Third Exception . -Conduct of any person touching any public question . -It is not defamation to express in  good  faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the  conduct  of  any  person  touching  any  public question, and respecting his character, so far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Illustration
It is not defamation in A to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting Z's conduct in petitioning Government on a  public  question,  in  signing  a  requisition  for  a  meeting  on  a  public  question,  in  presiding  or  attending  at  such  meeting,  in forming  or  joining  any  society  which  invites  the  public  support,  in  voting  or  canvassing  for  a  particular  candidate  for  any situation in the efficient discharge of the duties of which the public is interested.
Explanation . -A Justice of the Peace or other officer holding an enquiry in open Court preliminary to a trial in a Court of Justice, is a Court within the meaning of the above section.
Fourth  Exception . -Publication  of  reports  of  proceedings  of  courts. -It  is  not  defamation  to publish  substantially  true  report  of  the  proceedings  of  a  Court  of  Justice,  or  of  the  result  of  any  such proceedings.
Fifth  Exception . -Merits  of case decided  in  Court  or  conduct  of witnesses and  others concerned . -It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion whatever respecting the merits of any case, civil or criminal, which has been decided by a Court of Justice, or respecting the conduct of any person as a party, witness or agent, in any such case, or respecting the character of such person, as far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.
Illustrations
( b ) But if A says -' I do not believe what Z asserted at that trial because I know him to be a man without veracity ' ; A is not within this exception, inasmuch as the opinion which express of Z's character, is an opinion not founded on Z's conduct as a witness.
( a )  A  says -' I  think  Z's  evidence  on  that  trial  is  so  contradictory  that  he  must  be  stupid  or  dishonest. ' A  is  within  this exception if he says this in good faith, inasmuch as the opinion which he expresses respects Z's character as it appears in Z's conduct as a witness, and no farther.
Sixth Exception . -Merits of public performance . -It is not defamation to express in good faith any opinion respecting the merits of any performance which its author has submitted to the judgment of the public, or respecting the character of the author so far as his character appears in such performance, and no further.
Explanation . -A performance may be submitted to the judgment of the public expressly or by acts on the part of the author which imply such submission to the judgment of the public.
- ( a ) A person who publishes a book, submits that book to the judgment of the public.
- ( b ) A person who makes a speech in public, submits that speech to the judgment of the public.
- ( c ) An actor or singer who appears on a public stage, submits his acting or singing to the judgment of the public.
( d ) A says of a book published by Z -' Z ' s book is foolish; Z must be a weak man. Z's book is indecent; Z must be a man of  impure  mind ' .  A  is  within  the  exception,  if  he  says  this  in  good  faith,  inasmuch  as  the  opinion  which  he  expresses  of  Z respects Z's character only so far as it appears in Z's book, and no further.
( e ) But if A says ' I am not surprised that Z's book is foolish and indecent, for he is a weak man and a libertine ' . A is not within this exception, in as much as the opinion which he expresses of Z's character is an opinion not founded on Z's book.
Illustrations
Seventh  Exception . -Censure  passed  in  good  faith  by  person  having  lawful  authority  over another . -It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.
Illustration
A Judge censuring in good faith the conduct of a witness, or of an officer of the Court; a head of a department censuring in good  faith  those  who  are  under  his  orders,  a  parent  censuring  in  good  faith  a  child  in  the  presence  of  other  children;  a schoolmaster, whose authority is derived from a parent, censuring in good faith a pupil in the presence of other pupils; a master censuring  a  servant  in  good  faith  for  remissness  in  service;  a  banker  censuring  in  good  faith  the  cashier  of  his  bank  for  the conduct of such cashier as such cashier- are within this exception.
Eighth Exception . -Accusation preferred in good  faith to authorised  person . -It is not defamation  to  prefer  in  good  faith  an  accusation  against  any  person  to  any  of  those  who  have  lawful authority over that person with respect to the subject-matter of accusation.
If A in good faith accuses Z before a Magistrate; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a servant, to Z's master; if A in good faith complains of the conduct of Z, a child, to Z's father-A is within this exception.
Ninth  Exception . -Imputation  made  in  good  faith  by  person  for  protection  of  his  or  other's interests . -It  is  not  defamation  to  make  an  imputation  on  the  character  of  another  provided  that  the imputation be made in good faith for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good.
Illustrations
( a ) A, a shopkeeper, says to B, who manages his business -' Sell nothing to Z unless he pays you ready money, for I have no opinion of his honesty. ' A is within the exception, if he has made this imputation on Z in good faith for the protection of his own interests.
( b ) A, a Magistrate, in making a report to his own superior officer, casts an imputation on the character of Z. Here, if the imputation is made in good faith, and for the public good, A is within the exception.
Tenth Exception . -Caution intended for good of person to whom conveyed or for public good . -It is not defamation to convey a caution, in good faith, to one person against another, provided that such caution be intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed, or of some person in whom that person is interested, or for the public good.", 'Defamation . -Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.', 'Defamation. -( 1 ) Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible  representations,  makes  or  publishes  in  any  manner,  any  imputation  concerning  any  person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.']
response:
Yes. Under **BNS §356 (Defamation) Explanation 1**, it **“may amount to defamation to impute anything to a deceased person”** if (i) **“the imputation would harm the reputation of that person if living”** and (ii) **“is intended to be hurtful to the feelings of his family or other near relatives.”** [1]

The same position is reflected in **IPC §1 (Explanation 1)**: it may amount to defamation to impute anything to a deceased person if it would harm their reputation if living and is intended to be hurtful to the feelings of their family or other near relatives. [2]
reference: Yes. It may amount to defamation to impute something to a deceased person if the imputation would harm that person’s reputation if they were living, and it is intended to be hurtful to the feelings of the deceased person’s family or other near relatives.

Whether or not it is for the public good is a question of fact.', 'Exception 7. -It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.']
response:
It is **not considered defamation** to convey a warning to one person against another when **all** of the following conditions are satisfied:

1. The caution is conveyed **“in good faith”**; and  
2. The caution is **intended for the good** of:  
   - **the person to whom it is conveyed**, or  
   - **some person in whom that person is interested**, or  
   - **the public good**. [1]
reference: It is not defamation to convey a caution in good faith to one person against another, if the warning is intended for the good of the person receiving it, or of someone in whom that person is interested, or for the public good.

user_input: When is it not considered defamation for one person to criticize another’s conduct, and what must be the person’s state of mind?
retrieved_contexts: ['Exception 10. -It is not defamation to convey a caution, in good faith, to one person against another, provided that such caution be intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed, or of some person in whom that person is interested, or for the public good.', 'Illustrations\nSeventh  Exception . -Censure  passed  in  good  faith  by  person  having  lawful  authority  over another . -It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.', 'Exception 7. -It is not defamation in a person having over another any authority, either conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract made with that other, to pass in good faith any censure on the conduct of that other in matters to which such lawful authority relates.', 'Exception 9. -It is not defamation to make an imputation on the character of another provided that the imputation be made in good faith for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good.', 'Exception 5. -It  is  not  defamation  to  express  in  good  faith  any  opinion  whatever  respecting  the merits of any case, civil or criminal, which has been decided by a Court, or respecting the conduct of any person as a party, witness or agent, in any such case, or respecting the character of such person, as far as his character appears in that conduct, and no further.']
response:
It is not considered defamation when a person **criticizes another’s conduct** in the following situations under **BNS §356**:

1. **With lawful authority and in good faith (Exception 7):** when a person having authority (conferred by law or arising out of a lawful contract) passes in good faith a censure on the other’s conduct in matters to which that authority relates. [3]  
2. **To convey a good-faith caution (Exception 10):** when a person conveys, **in good faith**, a caution to one person against another, intended for the good of the person to whom it is conveyed (or someone interested in them), or for the public good. [1]  
3. **For protection of interests / public good (Exception 9):** when a person makes an imputation on the character of another **in good faith** for the protection of the interests of the person making it (or another), or for the public good. [4]  

In each of these, the required **state of mind** is **“good faith.”** [1, 3, 4]
reference: It is not defamation if the person has authority over the other—either granted by law or arising from a lawful contract—and, in good faith, passes censure on the other’s conduct in matters to which that authority relates.

user_input: A group of five people regularly plan and act together to commit dacoity. One member is arrested while the group is still only associated for that purpose (no robbery has yet occurred). Separately, another person commits a robbery on a highway at night (after sunset and before sunrise). What are the maximum punishments (imprisonment term and any possible extension) and whether fine is also applicable for each person?
retrieved_contexts: ['( 5 ) Whoever is one of five or more persons assembled for the purpose of committing dacoity, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.', '( 4 ) Whoever commits robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and, if the robbery be committed on the highway between sunset and sunrise, the imprisonment may be extended to fourteen years.', 'Dacoity  with  murder . -If  any  one  of  five  or  more  persons,  who  are  conjointly  committing dacoity,  commits murder in so committing dacoity, every one of those persons shall be punished with death, or 1 [imprisonment for life], or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.', 'Punishment  for  robbery . -Whoever  commits  robbery  shall  be  punished  with  rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and, if the robbery be committed on the highway between sunset and sunrise, the imprisonment may be extended to fourteen years.', '( 6 )  Whoever  belongs  to  a  gang  of  persons  associated  for  the  purpose  of  habitually  committing dacoity, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.']
response:
- **For each person in the group of five (associated/regularly planning together, no robbery yet):**  
  - Under **BNS §310(6) — Dacoity**: punishment is **imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years**, and **shall also be liable to fine**. [5]  
  - **Maximum imprisonment term:** **life imprisonment** (or **up to 10 years** under rigorous imprisonment). [5]  
  - **Fine:** **applicable** (“shall also be liable to fine”). [5]

- **For the person who commits robbery on a highway between sunset and sunrise:**  
  - Under **BNS §309(4) — Robbery**: punishment is **rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years**, and **shall also be liable to fine**; **if the robbery be committed on the highway between sunset and sunrise, the imprisonment may be extended to fourteen years**. [2]  
  - **Maximum imprisonment term:** **14 years** (extension). [2]  
  - **Fine:** **applicable** (“shall also be liable to fine”). [2]
reference: The person who belongs to a gang associated for habitually committing dacoity can be punished with imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, and is also liable to fine. The person who commits robbery on a highway between sunset and sunrise can be punished with rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, which may be extended up to 14 years, and is also liable to fine.

## IPC (Indian Penal Code) — §372: “Selling minor for purposes of prostitution, etc”
### (a) Victim’s status
- The provision applies to **“any person under the age of eighteen years”**. [1, 2]

### (b) Accused’s intent or knowledge
- The act is punishable if the accused acts **with intent** that the person “shall at any age be employed or used for the purpose of prostitution or illicit intercourse with any person” or “for any unlawful and immoral purpose,” **or** if the accused **knows it to be likely** that the person will at any age be employed or used for any such purpose. [1, 2]

### (c) Conduct covered
- The conduct covered is: **“sells, lets to hire, or otherwise disposes of”** the minor. [1, 2]
- **Explanation I** adds a presumption: when a female under eighteen is sold/let for hire/disposed of **to a prostitute or to any person who keeps or manages a brothel**, the disposer is **presumed (until contrary is proved)** to have disposed with the intent that she be used for prostitution. [1]

### (d) Definition of “illicit intercourse”
- IPC §372 contains **Explanation II**: **“illicit intercourse” means sexual intercourse between persons not united by marriage or by any union or tie… recognised by the personal law or custom… as constituting… a quasi-marital relation.** [1, 4]

---

## BNS (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) — §98: “Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc”
### (a) Victim’s status
- The provision applies to **“any child”**. [3]

### (b) Accused’s intent or knowledge
- The requirement is the same structure as IPC: intent that the child “shall at any age be employed or used for” prostitution or “illicit intercourse,” or for an “unlawful and immoral purpose,” **or knowledge** that it is likely the child will be employed/used for any such purpose. [3]

### (c) Conduct covered
- The conduct covered is: **“sells, lets to hire, or otherwise disposes of”** the child. [3]

### (d) Definition of “illicit intercourse” / whether retained
- BNS §98 includes **Explanation 2**, defining **“illicit intercourse”** in substantially the same terms as IPC §372 Explanation II: sexual intercourse between persons not united by marriage or by any recognised union/tie, as constituting a **“quasi-marital relation.”** [5]

---

## Key comparison (as asked)
1. **Victim status:**  
   - **IPC §372:** “person under the age of eighteen years” [1, 2]

response:
### IPC (older law): “Putting person in fear… in order to commit extortion” (IPC §389)
- **Wording / purpose element:** The section applies *“in order to the committing of extortion”*—i.e., **the accused must put (or attempt to put) a person in fear of an accusation for the purpose of extortion**. [1]
- **Range of offences covered (by accusation):** The fear/accusation must relate to an offence punishable with:
  - **death**, or **1 [imprisonment for life]**, or
  - **imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years**. [1]
- **Special mention:** If the offence be punishable under **section 377**, it *“may be punished with 1 [imprisonment for life].”* [1]
- **No mention of inducing another person:** IPC §389 (as shown) focuses on putting/attempting to put “any person” in fear of an accusation; **it does not expressly include an element about attempting to induce any other person** to commit the offence. [1]

---

### BNS (newer law): “Extortion” (BNS §308(6) and §308(7))
#### BNS §308(6) (fear of accusation)
- **Wording / purpose element:** Uses similar framing: *“in order to the committing of extortion”* and provides for punishment where the person **“puts or attempts to put any person in fear”** of an accusation. [2]
- **Range of offences covered (by accusation):** Same set as in IPC §389 for this part—offences punishable with **death**, **imprisonment for life**, or **imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years**. [2]
- **No special mention (in this subsection):** BNS §308(6), as shown, does **not** include the IPC §389 special “section 377” mention. [2]

#### BNS §308(7) (express extension to “attempted to induce”)
- **Additional element added in wording:** BNS §308(7) expressly includes not only accusation/fear for extortion, but also where the accused **“having attempted to induce any other person to commit such offence”**. [4]
- **Range of offences covered:** It again covers offences punishable with **death**, **imprisonment for life**, or **imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years**. [4]
- **No “section 377” special mention in this subsection:** As shown, this subsection does **not** replicate the IPC §389 “if punishable under section 377… may be punished with imprisonment for life” clause. [4]

---

### Key differences in wording/scope (as between IPC §389 and BNS §308)
1. **Purpose requirement (“in order to the committing of extortion”)** is present in both IPC §389 and BNS §308(6). [1, 2]
2. **Offence range for the accusation** (death / imprisonment for life / up to ten years) is the same for IPC §389 and BNS §308(6). [1, 2]
3. **Special mention of offences under the old Code:** IPC §389 includes a special clause for offences **punishable under section 377**. [1] The provided BNS text shown for §308(6) and §308(7) does **not** contain that “section 377” special mention. [2, 4]
4. **Inducing another person:** The newer law (BNS §308(7)) **expressly adds** coverage where the accused has **“attempted to induce any other person to commit such offence.”** [4] The IPC §389 text shown **does not** include this “attempted to induce” element. [1]

If you want, I can also compare IPC §388 (extortion by threat of accusation) with the corresponding BNS wording in the provided context.
reference: Both laws punish extortion committed by putting (or attempting to put) a person in fear of an accusation of having committed/attempted an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, or up to ten years, with punishment up to ten years and fine. The IPC provision expressly includes “in order to committing of extortion” and also contains a special clause for offences punishable under IPC section 377 (allowing imprisonment for life). The BNS provision removes that IPC section 377 special mention and adds an explicit element that extortion includes attempting to induce any other person to commit such offence.

### IPC (Indian Penal Code)
A person who **joins or continues in an unlawful assembly after it has been ordered to disperse** is treated under **IPC §145**.

**(i) “Commanded to disperse” as an element**
- It is an express element: the person must join/continue **“knowing that such unlawful assembly has been commanded in the manner prescribed by law to disperse.”** [1]

**(ii) Additional conditions**
- The assembly must be an **“unlawful assembly.”** [1]
- The person must act **while “knowing”** the assembly has been **commanded to disperse** in the **manner prescribed by law.** [1]

**(iii) Punishment framework**
- **“imprisonment of either description for a term which may extent to two years, or with fine, or with both.”** [1]

Under **the Indian Penal Code (IPC)** and **the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)**, persons **subject to specified Army/Navy/Air Force service laws are excluded from punishment under the general code/Sanhita for offences defined in the chapter dealing with those offences**:

## 1) IPC (Chapter on offences relating to the Army, Navy and Air Force)
**IPC §139 — “Persons subject to certain Acts”** states:  
“No person subject to **the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950)**, the **Naval Discipline Act**, **the Indian Navy (Discipline) Act, 1934 (34 of 1934)**, **the Air Force Act** … **the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950)**, is subject to punishment under this Code for any of the offences defined in this Chapter.” [2]

## 2) BNS (corresponding chapter)
**BNS §167 — “Persons subject to certain Acts”** states:  
“No person subject to **the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950)**, **the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950)** and **the Navy Act, 1957 (62 of 1957)**, or shall be subject to punishment under this Sanhita for any of the offences defined in this Chapter.” [1]

## Comparison: named service laws and changes in wording/list
- **Common exclusion purpose/wording (substance):**  
  Both provisions exclude specified persons from being “subject to punishment under” the **Code/Sanhita** for “any of the offences defined in this Chapter.” [1, 2]
- **Specific service laws named:**
  - **IPC §139** names (as reflected in the text):  
    - **Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950)** [2]  
    - **Naval Discipline Act** and **Indian Navy (Discipline) Act, 1934 (34 of 1934)** [2]  
    - **Air Force Act** and **Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950)** [2]
  - **BNS §167** names instead:  
    - **Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950)** [1]  
    - **Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950)** [1]  
    - **Navy Act, 1957 (62 of 1957)** [1]
- **What changed (from the provided extracts):**
  - The **Army** and **Air Force 1950 (46 of 1950 / 45 of 1950)** exclusions remain, but  
  - The **naval service-law listing changes**: IPC lists **“Naval Discipline Act”** and **“Indian Navy (Discipline) Act, 1934 (34 of 1934)”**, while BNS lists **“Navy Act, 1957 (62 of 1957)”**. [1, 2]
  - The **phrasing** differs slightly in form: IPC says “**is subject to punishment under this Code**,” whereas BNS says “**or shall be subject to punishment under this Sanhita**,” but both refer to the same chapter-based offences. [1, 2]
reference: Both provisions exclude persons governed by specified service laws from being punished under the general criminal code/sanhita for offences defined in that chapter. IPC names the Army Act (1950), the Naval Discipline Act (and the Indian Navy (Discipline) Act, 1934), and the Air Force Act (and the Air Force Act, 1950). BNS instead names the Air Force Act, 1950, the Army Act, 1950, and the Navy Act, 1957, replacing the older naval discipline/Indian Navy (Discipline) Act references with the Navy Act, 1957 and simplifying the list.

user_input: In the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, what is the corresponding offence for “omission to give notice or information to a public servant by a person legally bound to give it” under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and how do the punishments compare to the Indian Penal Code version?
response:
Under the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNS)**, the corresponding offence to **“omission to give notice or information to a public servant by a person legally bound to give it”** (under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita) is **BNS §211**. [1]

### BNS §211 (corresponding offence) — punishment
- Where no special circumstance applies: **simple imprisonment up to one month**, or **fine up to five thousand rupees**, or **both**. [1]
- Where the notice/information relates to:
  - **commission of an offence**, or
  - **preventing the commission of an offence**, or
  - **apprehension of an offender**: **simple imprisonment up to six months**, or **fine up to ten thousand rupees**, or **both**. [1]
- Where required by an order under **section 394 of BNS, 2023**: **imprisonment of either description up to six months**, or **fine up to one thousand rupees**, or **both**. [1]

### Comparison with IPC §176 (Indian Penal Code)
IPC §176 provides the same basic structure, but with lower fines:

- General case: **simple imprisonment up to one month**, or **fine up to five hundred rupees**, or **both**. [2]
- Special case (offence/ prevention/ apprehension): **simple imprisonment up to six months**, or **fine up to one thousand rupees**, or **both**. [2]
- Also includes an additional clause (in IPC): where required by an order under **sub-section (1) of section 565 of CrPC, 1898**, punishment is **imprisonment of either description up to six months**, or **fine up to one thousand rupees**, or **both**. [2]

**Key punishment differences (fines):**
- General case fine: **BNS up to Rs. 5,000** vs **IPC up to Rs. 500**. [1, 2]
- Special case fine: **BNS up to Rs. 10,000** vs **IPC up to Rs. 1,000**. [1, 2]
- BNS’s “section 394 order” fine cap is **Rs. 1,000** (IPC’s corresponding order clause also shows **Rs. 1,000**). [1, 2]
reference: The BNS has the corresponding offence of omission to give notice or information to a public servant by a person legally bound to give it. The structure is similar, but the BNS increases fines: for general omission the fine limit rises from ₹500 (IPC) to ₹5,000 (BNS); for omission related to an offence/prevention/apprehension it rises from ₹1,000 (IPC) to ₹10,000 (BNS). The imprisonment ranges (up to 1 month or up to 6 months) remain the same, with a separate clause for notices required by a BNS order.

Under the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)**, the equivalent of **IPC §213 (Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment)** is **BNS §250 (Taking gift, etc.)**. [1, 2]

**Notable change in how punishment is stated:** In the provided documents, **IPC §213 includes detailed punishment ranges** based on the maximum punishment for the underlying offence (death ⇒ up to seven years and fine; imprisonment for life/ten years ⇒ up to three years and fine; other cases ⇒ up to one-fourth of the longest term and/or fine). [1]  
However, **BNS §250 is only shown up to “shall, -” and does not include the corresponding punishment wording** in the provided context. [2]
reference: The BNS has the corresponding offence of taking a gift/gratification (or restitution) to conceal an offence or screen someone from legal punishment. The substantive punishment ranges are the same as under the IPC, but the BNS presents the punishment conditions in a clearer illustrative/lettered format (a), (b), (c) rather than the IPC’s inline conditional wording.

### 3) Other material elements / phrasing changes
- **Common element (“knowing”):** Both use the same mental element wording:  
  “**knowing** the same to have been taken in the commission of …” [1, 2]

The only substantive change is the cross-referenced offences: IPC refers to the offences in sections 125 and 126, while BNS refers to the corresponding offences in sections 153 and 154.

user_input: Under the Indian Penal Code and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, how does the law describe the court’s power to decide whether an imprisonment sentence is rigorous, simple, or a mix of both? Please compare the wording and explain what, if anything, changed between the two Acts in this regard.
response:
Under both Acts, when an offender is “punishable with imprisonment which may be of either description,” the court can decide in the sentence whether the imprisonment is:

- **Wholly rigorous**, or **wholly simple**, or
- **Partly rigorous and the rest simple**.  
[BNS §7] [3]

### Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023
**BNS §7** states (verbatim):  
“In every case in which an offender is punishable with imprisonment which may be of either description, it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct in the sentence that such imprisonment shall be wholly rigorous, or that such imprisonment shall be wholly simple, or that any part of such imprisonment shall be rigorous and the rest simple.” [3]

### Indian Penal Code (IPC) (comparison)
The provided context shows **IPC §60** with the **same wording**:  
“In every case in which an offender is punishable with imprisonment which may be of either description, it shall be competent to the Court which sentences such offender to direct in the sentence that such imprisonment shall be wholly rigorous, or that such imprisonment shall be wholly simple, or that any part of such imprisonment shall be rigorous and the rest simple.” [4]

### What changed between the two Acts (based on the provided documents)
Based on the provided excerpts, **nothing changes in the phrasing** about the court’s power: the **wording in BNS §7 and IPC §60 is identical** on this point. [3, 4]
reference: Both Acts state that when an offender is punishable with imprisonment of either description, the sentencing court may direct the imprisonment to be wholly rigorous, wholly simple, or partly rigorous and the rest simple; the wording is substantively the same with no meaningful change.
